replies.author: PacosTacos42069
replies.body:
I believe so, yes. It’s not in there to “prevent” movement during transport. 
Because of this horrible incident US Congress passed “The Tylenol Bill,” establishing Federal guidelines for manufacturers to make all such products tamper-proof or “tamper resistant.” 

Also, something to note too is that they never found the person who did the poisonings. There were wannabes that came forward but they were all ruled out as suspects.

replies.author: FencingFemmeFatale
replies.body:
James W. Lewis sent an extortion letter to Johnson & Johnson demanding 1 million dollars to stop the spree of killings in the Chicago area that were caused by Tylenol capsules laced with cyanide.

After his arrest, he claimed that he wasn’t *actually* responsible for the Tylenol murders and the extortion letter was just an emotional outburst, despite knowing details about the poisoning that hadn’t been made public at the time. He was convicted of extortion but they didn’t have enough evidence to charge him with murder and the killer was never identified.

replies.author: Rust_Coal
replies.body: James Lewis was also a prime suspect in the murder/missing person case of an elderly neighbor that he/his wife did taxes for before the Tylenol case. He definitely had the sociopathy but the recent Netflix documentary about the Tylenol murders also provides good evidence for other suspects including inadvertent/accidental poisoning from within the plant.
